Then came the mid-semester exam. No notebook, no Sachin. Kalyani sat staring at a circuit she had seen solved many times and couldn't begin. She came out pale and went straight to his room. 'I don't know how to start any of them. I only know how to watch you do them.'

In their PG in Kothrud, Neelam had become Hansa's go-to for programming. Whenever Hansa's code broke, she'd slide her laptop across the kitchen table and Neelam would fix it in a minute. It felt kind. It was quicker than explaining.
By November, Hansa had stopped reading error messages at all. 'Neelam di, it's red again,' she'd call, and Neelam would come.
Then Hansa had a live coding round for an internship. Forty minutes, camera on, no help. Her program threw an error in the first ten minutes. She stared at it. She realised she had never once fixed an error on her own. She typed, deleted, typed. The interviewer waited, then said, 'Let's stop here.'
That night Hansa said quietly, 'I think you fixed too much for me.' Neelam, drying a plate, didn't argue.
